## Why Pollination Matters {background-color="#1B4332"}

*Pourquoi la pollinisation compte*

::: {.notes}
Transition, ~5 sec.
:::

## A problem plants can't solve by moving

- Plants are rooted in place — but reproduction needs pollen to
  travel from anther to stigma
- Two basic options: **self-pollination** (pollen fertilizes the same
  individual) or **cross-pollination** (pollen moves between
  individuals)
- Neither option is free — each comes with a genetic and ecological
  trade-off

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Set up the trade-off before naming it explicitly on the next
slide.
:::

## Selfing vs. outcrossing

| | **Self-pollination** | **Cross-pollination** |
|---|---|---|
| Reliability | Guaranteed — no vector or mate needed | Depends on a vector reaching a compatible mate |
| Genetic diversity | Low — risk of inbreeding depression | High — more robust, adaptable offspring |
| Cost | Cheap, reproductive assurance | Costly: must attract and pay a vector |

- Many plants actively **avoid** self-pollination: anthers and
  stigma maturing at different times (dichogamy), spatial separation
  within the flower (herkogamy), or outright genetic
  self-incompatibility
- ~90% of flowering plant species rely at least partly on an animal
  vector for cross-pollination

::: {.notes}
~2 min. The mechanisms preventing selfing are worth naming even
briefly - they show how strongly most plants are investing in
outcrossing despite the cost and unreliability of needing a vector.
:::

## Pollination agents: abiotic

- **Wind** (anemophily) — grasses, conifers, oaks: huge quantities of
  small, light pollen, inconspicuous flowers, no reward needed at all
- **Water** (hydrophily) — rare, mostly aquatic plants (e.g.
  *Vallisneria*)
- Abiotic pollination is a numbers game: no signaling, no reward, just
  massive overproduction to compensate for how inefficient it is

::: {.notes}
~1 min. Useful contrast point: abiotic pollination needs none of the
signal/reward machinery the rest of today is about, precisely because
it doesn't rely on an organism that has to be persuaded.
:::

## Pollination agents: biotic

- **Insects** (entomophily) — bees, flies, beetles, moths, butterflies
- **Birds** (ornithophily) — hummingbirds, sunbirds
- **Bats** (chiropterophily), and more rarely other mammals and even
  some reptiles
- An estimated **87% of flowering plant species** depend on animal
  pollinators — and animal pollination underpins roughly a third of
  global food crop production by value

**Attracting and rewarding a mobile animal is expensive — which is
exactly why the rest of today is about how plants pay for it.**

::: {.notes}
~1.5 min. Bridge directly into "the flower as a marketplace." The 87%
figure is from Ollerton, Winfree & Tarrant (2011) - worth citing if
asked.
:::
